text: Plugins are add-ons that you create to give ChatDBT reusable instructions, tools, or both. And you've got to kind of think of a plugin as a package. And inside that package, you can add skills which define the steps and the rules, and for example output formats that ChatDBT has to follow, and app connections, which let ChatDBT retrieve information or take supported actions in other apps. A plugin can contain one or more skills, app connections, or both. And once they're installed, you can select a plugin by typing the add symbol in any conversation instead of pasting the same detailed instructions every time. So in this demo, I'm going to build Larry, a leadership update creator, and Larry's job will be to turn project information into a short weekly update for senior leaders. Its skill will define how the update should be written, while Google Drive and Slack app connections can give Larry access to the source information it needs. And that means that Larry knows both what to do, but also when needed where to get the information. So on the web, I'm going to open ChatDBT's plugin page at chatdbt.com slash plugins, and select the plus button and then create plugin. ChatDBT will now open up a work conversation with the plugin creator selected. You can also simply open it by typing add plugin creator and selecting it in a work conversation. So now I'm going to give the plugin creator the instructions for Larry, which includes its character, what the objectives are, the do's and don'ts, and the final desired outputs. And I'm also going to mention that I want to add Google Drive and Slack as the connected apps. So you always add these apps to a plugin conversationally. There isn't a menu on the plugin page where you can click and then select some of these apps. So you always have to tell the plugin creator which apps that you want included when you create the plugin. If you want to add another app later, you can return to the plugin creator, mention the existing plugin and then ask it to add the app, but all conversationally. So now that I've done the plugin creator will create Larry and it will give me a link to the plugin page. Here I can quickly check that the skill actually matches what I asked for and then select install plugin. Now depending on how the plugin is created, Chatchity may install it automatically or prompt you to install it yourself. And once it's installed, I can open up a new conversation, type add Larry, and then ask something like, draft this week's leadership update by checking Slack and Drive. And then Larry will return the briefing. Now of course I'm going to check the information, make sure it matches my notes, make sure the four sections I asked for are here and make sure it didn't invent any missing details. And if something needs changing as I'm using this plugin over time, I can return to the plugin creator and then update the plugin and or the skill and then test again. So for plugins, the distinction is simple. The skill tells Larry how to do the job. The app connection gives Larry access to the information or the tools that it may need and the plugin and packages all those pieces together. If you just need a reusable instruction for a task, then a skill may be enough. A plugin becomes useful when you want to package skills together with apps or with other capabilities or distribute the whole workflow as one installable experience. The plugin creator is available on any Chattavity plan, but individual plugin capabilities still depend on your plan, your workspace, your role, region, and the included capabilities. And your workspace admin controls access to plugin creation, sharing, and publishing. So if you don't see Create Plugin, then check with your admin.
